Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Vignette:
Adebayo sits with a stillness that seems at odds with the tension in his hands, which are clasped so tightly the knuckles are white. At seventy-seven, he has always carried himself with the quiet authority befitting a man who has led a large high school for over two decades. But in the eight months since the assault, that authority has felt like a costume he can no longer inhabit. The incident itself was brutally simple. Walking home from a late board meeting, two young men cornered him in the poorly lit stairwell of a parking garage. The reek of cheap liquor was the first thing he registered, a cloying cloud that seemed to stick to the back of his throat. They wanted his wallet and his watch, a retirement gift from his wife. Adebayo, a man accustomed to de-escalating conflict with words, tried to reason with them. This, he is now certain, was his fatal error. His calm voice only seemed to incite them. One shoved him against the concrete wall while the other pinned his arms. The feeling of being completely overpowered, of his body being moved and manipulated against his will, was a profound violation. He was forced to his knees, his face pressed into the grimy floor, while they took his things. He remembers the sound of their slurred laughter echoing in the stairwell long after they were gone.

In the weeks that followed, Adebayo tried to return to his life, but the world had rearranged itself into a landscape of threats. At school, an environment he once commanded with ease, he found himself unable to enter a room without his eyes immediately flicking to the exits. During a fire drill, the sudden rush of students from a classroom behind him sent a jolt of pure terror through his body; he flinched so violently that a teacher rushed to his side, asking if he was alright. He has come to believe he is fundamentally broken, that he can no longer rely on his own judgment or strength. The memory of his failed attempt to talk his way out of the assault plays on a loop, convincing him the event only happened because of the way he acted. If he had been stronger, louder, different, it could have been avoided. This belief has curdled into a wider conviction that he cannot rely on anyone, a feeling reinforced by the memory of his own cries for help going unanswered in the empty garage.

The memories of the attack are unpredictable visitors. Sometimes, they arrive with a wave of incapacitating grief that forces him to retreat to his office and lock the door, overwhelmed by a sorrow so vast it feels like it could drown him. At other times, the memory is purely sensory; while reviewing budget spreadsheets, he will suddenly hear the phantom sound of that mocking, drunken laughter, as sharp and clear as if the men were in the room with him. Perhaps most unsettling are the moments when he can recall the event with a flat, clinical detachment. When his wife, Funke, found him staring blankly at the wall one evening and asked what was wrong, he recounted the assault with no emotion at all, as if narrating a story about a stranger. The fear in her eyes was a mirror of his own.

His life has shrunk. He no longer attends evening school functions or community fundraisers, especially if alcohol might be served. The smell of hand sanitizer on a student can make his heart hammer against his ribs. He has started delegating parent meetings that he anticipates will be contentious, unable to bear the feeling of being in a situation he cannot entirely control. His staff, once accustomed to his steady presence, now speak of his distance and unpredictability. It was Funke who finally insisted he seek help, after finding him standing frozen in their hallway, his body rigid with fear because she had come up quietly behind him to offer him a cup of tea. Adebayo is here now not because he believes he can be fixed, but because he is terrified of the man he is becoming—a stranger in his own home, a ghost in the hallways of his own school.
